items.title: What is Web Scraping and BeautifulSoup?
items.content:
Web scraping is the automated process of extracting data from websites. When you visit a webpage, your browser receives HTML, which is a tree-like structure of tags such as , , ,

, and

. BeautifulSoup is a Python library that parses this HTML and lets you navigate and search the tree easily. To begin, install it with: pip install beautifulsoup4. Then, import the library and pass an HTML string or a response object to BeautifulSoup. For example, if you have a string of HTML content, you can create a soup object like this: ```python from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '

Hello World

' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') ``` The 'html.parser' tells BeautifulSoup to use Python's built-in parser. Once you have the soup object, you can call methods like .find() to locate the first matching tag, or .find_all() to collect every matching tag. This makes it simple to pull out text, links, or images from a page without manually reading the raw HTML.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly creates a BeautifulSoup object from an HTML string using the built-in parser?
items.explanation: The first argument to BeautifulSoup must be the HTML source, and the second argument must be the name of the parser to use. 'html.parser' is the correct string for Python's built-in parser. Omitting the parser name works in some cases but is not the explicit, recommended syntax shown in this lesson.

items.title: Common BeautifulSoup Syntax Patterns
items.content:
Once you have a soup object, you can extract data using tags, attributes, and text. A tag represents an HTML element, and you can access it by name. The .text attribute returns only the visible text inside a tag, stripping out nested tags. The .get('attribute') method retrieves the value of a specific HTML attribute, such as 'href' in an anchor tag. Here is a practical example: ```python from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
Click here42
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') link = soup.find('a') url = link.get('href') text = link.text number = soup.find('span').text print(url) # 'https://example.com' print(text) # 'Click here' print(number) # '42' ``` Notice that .text gives you clean strings, while .get('href') gives you the raw attribute value. You can chain these methods to drill down into deeply nested structures.

items.prompt:
Given the HTML snippet '

Price: $10

', which sequence of BeautifulSoup calls correctly extracts the price text 'Price: $10'?
items.explanation: To locate the paragraph with class 'note', you must pass class_='note' as a keyword argument to find. The .text attribute, not .get('text'), returns the inner text of the tag. Therefore, soup.find('p', class_='note').text is the correct expression.

items.prompt: Match the BeautifulSoup method to its purpose: retrieving all anchor tags, extracting visible text, and getting an attribute value.
items.explanation: find_all retrieves every matching tag, .text returns visible text, and .get retrieves an attribute value such as 'href'. These three correspond in order to the three purposes described in the prompt.

items.prompt: Which of the following is a common pitfall when scraping with BeautifulSoup?
options: Using .text when you actually need the raw HTML markup
Forgetting to install requests before importing BeautifulSoup
Using single quotes instead of double quotes in Python strings
Calling .find_all() on a string instead of a soup object
items.correct_answer: Using .text when you actually need the raw HTML markup
items.explanation: A frequent mistake is assuming .text gives you everything. If you need nested tags, comments, or raw markup, .text strips them away. You should use .prettify() or access the tag directly when raw structure matters. The other options describe either unrelated issues or not typical pitfalls for BeautifulSoup itself.

First

Second

""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') paragraphs = soup.find_all('p') for p in paragraphs: print(p.text) ``` What is the exact output produced by this script when executed?
items.explanation:
The script parses the HTML, finds all

tags, and iterates through them. The .text attribute returns the inner text of each tag, printing 'First' on one line and 'Second' on the next with a newline separator.

items.prompt: Given this Python code using BeautifulSoup to extract links from a mock HTML page: ```python from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """HomeAbout""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') links = soup.find_all('a', href=True) for link in links: print(link['href']) ``` What is the exact output produced by this script when executed?
items.explanation: The script finds all <a> tags that have an href attribute, then accesses the 'href' key of each tag to print the URL. The output is the two URLs on separate lines.

items.prompt:
Consider the following Python code that scrapes a list of items from HTML: ```python from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """
  • Apple
  • Banana
  • Cherry
    • """ soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') items = soup.select('.item') for item in items: print(item.get_text().strip()) ``` What is the exact output produced by this script when executed?
items.explanation: The select method with '.item' finds all <li> elements with class 'item'. The loop calls get_text().strip() on each, removing whitespace and printing each fruit name on a separate line.

items.title: Analyzing BeautifulSoup Output
items.content:
When working with BeautifulSoup, it is essential to understand how the library parses HTML and how methods like find_all, select, and .text interact. In the following example, we parse a simple document and extract heading and paragraph elements. The .text attribute strips all HTML tags and returns only the human-readable content. Notice how nested tags are flattened: if a paragraph contains a element, .text still returns the combined text without markup. Understanding this behavior helps you avoid common pitfalls such as expecting raw HTML when you actually need cleaned text, or vice versa. Always verify the type of object returned—BeautifulSoup returns a list for find_all and a generator-like result for select—because this affects how you iterate and index the results. Below is a representative code block: ```python from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """

Title

Hello world

""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') heading = soup.find('h1') paragraph = soup.find('p') print(heading.text) print(paragraph.text) ``` The output is 'Title' followed by 'Hello world', demonstrating that .text aggregates all descendant text nodes and removes tags.

items.title: Step-by-Step Execution Trace
items.content:
Tracing execution with BeautifulSoup involves following how the parser builds the internal tree and how each method call traverses that tree. Consider the snippet below. At each step, note the value of the variable and the structure of the parsed tree. The trace helps solidify understanding of why certain methods return lists, tags, or strings. ```python from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """
  • One
  • Two
  • Three
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') items = soup.find_all('li') first = items[0] print(first.name) print(first.text) ``` Execution trace: 1. BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') creates a parse tree with a
    root containing three
  • children. 2. soup.find_all('li') returns a list of three
  • tag objects. 3. items[0] selects the first
  • tag object. 4. first.name returns the string 'li'. 5. first.text returns 'One'. The final printed output is 'li' on the first line and 'One' on the second line.

micro_lesson.title: Diagnosing BeautifulSoup Parsing Errors
micro_lesson.content:
When scraping a webpage, a common runtime error is `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'find'`. This occurs when `soup.find()` returns `None`, usually because the selector did not match any element. Another frequent mistake is passing an HTML string directly to `BeautifulSoup` without specifying a parser, which defaults to `html.parser` but may fail on malformed markup. Always verify the HTTP response status code before parsing, and use `soup.find_all()` when multiple matches are expected. Below is an example of a faulty scraper that crashes on a missing tag.

```python
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

url = 'https://example.com/page'
response = requests.get(url)
soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, 'html.parser')

# This line crashes if the tag is absent
price = soup.find('span', class_='price').text
print(price)
```

To fix this, check if the result is `None` before accessing `.text`, or use a default value.

items.prompt: The code below attempts to extract the first paragraph from a webpage, but it raises an error when the paragraph tag is missing. Fix the code so it safely returns an empty string instead of crashing.
items.starter_code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def get_first_paragraph(url):
    r = requests.get(url)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
    p = soup.find('p')
    return p.text

print(get_first_paragraph('https://example.com/missing'))
items.solution_code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def get_first_paragraph(url):
    r = requests.get(url)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
    p = soup.find('p')
    if p is None:
        return ''
    return p.text

print(get_first_paragraph('https://example.com/missing'))
items.hint: Check whether `p` is `None` before calling `.text` on it.
items.explanation:
The original code assumes a `

` tag always exists. By adding `if p is None: return ''`, we prevent the `AttributeError` and make the function robust against missing content.

items.prompt: A scraper is designed to collect all links from a page, but it fails when some `<a>` tags lack an `href` attribute. Correct the code so it skips invalid links and returns only valid URLs.
items.starter_code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
HomeBrokenAbout
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') links = [a['href'] for a in soup.find_all('a')] print(links)
items.solution_code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
HomeBrokenAbout
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') links = [a['href'] for a in soup.find_all('a') if a.has_attr('href')] print(links)
items.hint: Use `has_attr('href')` to filter out `<a>` tags that do not contain an `href`.
items.explanation: List comprehensions with `a['href']` throw a `KeyError` when `href` is missing. The `if a.has_attr('href')` guard ensures only tags with the attribute are processed.

micro_lesson.title: Runtime Errors in Scraping Pipelines
micro_lesson.content:
Runtime errors often surface only after a script runs for several minutes. A typical scenario is a `requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` caused by a timeout or a blocked IP. Another runtime pitfall is decoding issues: if the server returns bytes with an unexpected encoding, `response.text` may produce garbled characters. BeautifulSoup handles most encodings automatically, but you should still inspect `response.encoding` and pass it explicitly to `BeautifulSoup` when needed. Below is a snippet that crashes due to a missing network timeout.

```python
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

url = 'https://slow-site.example'
resp = requests.get(url)
soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.content, 'html.parser')
title = soup.title.string
print(title)
```

Adding `timeout=10` to `requests.get()` prevents indefinite hangs.

items.prompt: The function below is supposed to return a list of product names, but it incorrectly returns the entire text of each `<div>`, including nested tags. Rewrite the logic so it extracts only the clean text of each product name.
items.starter_code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
Product A
Product B
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') products = [div.text for div in soup.find_all('div')] print(products)
items.solution_code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
Product A
Product B
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') products = [div.get_text(strip=True) for div in soup.find_all('div')] print(products)
items.hint: Use `get_text(strip=True)` to remove extra whitespace and nested tag artifacts.
items.explanation: While `.text` works, `get_text(strip=True)` is more explicit for cleaning whitespace. In this simple case both produce the same result, but the intent of extracting clean product names is clearer with `get_text`.

items.prompt: Refactor the following scraper to improve readability, reduce redundant parsing, and add caching so repeated requests to the same URL do not hit the network again. Return a dictionary mapping each URL to its extracted titles.
items.starter_code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def scrape(urls):
    results = {}
    for u in urls:
        r = requests.get(u)
        s = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
        t = s.title.string
        results[u] = t
    return results

urls = ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com']
print(scrape(urls))
items.solution_code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

_cache = {}

def scrape(urls):
    results = {}
    for u in urls:
        if u in _cache:
            results[u] = _cache[u]
            continue
        r = requests.get(u, timeout=10)
        s = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
        t = s.title.string
        _cache[u] = t
        results[u] = t
    return results

urls = ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com']
print(scrape(urls))
test_cases: scrape(['https://a.com', 'https://a.com']) should return the same title for both calls without a second network request
scrape([]) should return an empty dictionary
items.hint: Store parsed results in a module-level dictionary keyed by URL, and check the cache before calling `requests.get`.
items.explanation: The refactored version avoids redundant HTTP calls by caching results in `_cache`. It also adds a `timeout` for safety and separates concerns by checking the cache before network I/O, improving both performance and reliability.
